lesson.text: Quick memory: what does a lintel do? (It carries the bricks over an opening.) Today: a small house.
A square corner with 3, 4, 5: mark 60 cm along one wall and 80 cm along the other. The diagonal must be 100 cm, because 3 x 3 + 4 x 4 = 5 x 5.
Corners first: builders raise the corners, then fill in between along a line stretched from corner to corner.
At a door or a window the rows end with half bricks, so the joints still stagger.
A lintel needs at least 15 cm resting on the wall at each end, to pass the weight down into the wall.
Rafters make the roof's frame; tiles go on from the bottom up. A steeper roof sheds rain faster.
Try it in the world: open Real Builder and build your house. Then look for lintels on real houses with a grown-up.

exercises.hint: Then a line runs between them.
exercises.explain: True: corners first, then the rows between.
Rafters make the frame; tiles cover it.

exercises.prompt: A lintel needs only 1 cm on the wall at each end.
exercises.hint: It carries a lot of weight.
exercises.explain: False: at least 15 cm at each end.

exercises.prompt: Pegs 60 cm and 80 cm from a corner: how long is the diagonal for a square corner, in cm?
A front of 315 cm, at 22.5 cm a brick: how many bricks long?
Why are there half bricks at the sides of a window?
exercises.explain: Half bricks keep the joints staggered right up to the opening.

exercises.hint: Which ones are up on top?
exercises.explain: Lintels and bricks are in the wall; rafters and tiles make the roof.

exercises.prompt: A window is 91 cm wide. Its lintel rests 15 cm on each side. How long is it at least, in cm?
A wall is 28 rows high, at 7.5 cm a row. How high is it, in cm?
Pegs 30 cm and 40 cm from a corner: what diagonal makes it square?
